deep.reconstruction:
The page holds six separate notes. They read like a list of problems and remarks, probably from about 1893–97: Appell's Traité vol. 1 appeared in 1893, and Klein's α,β,γ,δ for the top date from 1895–97.

(1) END OF THE PLANE MINKOWSKI PROBLEM (continued from the previous page). Prescribe the curvature of a closed convex curve as a function of the tangent slope p = y':
  κ = y''/(1+p^2)^{3/2} = f(p).
Then dp/dx = g(p), where g(p) := f(p)(1+p^2)^{3/2}. Separating variables gives
  x = ∫ dp/g(p) = F(p) + const,
and similarly (my addition) y = ∫ p dp/g(p) + const'. Hilbert says the constant is fixed by requiring that the curve closes.
My completion: use the normal angle θ and the radius of curvature ρ(θ) = 1/κ(θ). The curve is z(θ) = ∫ ρ(θ) e^{iθ} dθ (with z = x+iy). It closes if and only if ∫_0^{2π} ρ(θ) cos θ dθ = ∫_0^{2π} ρ(θ) sin θ dθ = 0. Under that condition the curve is unique up to translation. In the parametrisation by p, the curve splits into an upper and a lower arc, each with its own constants. Matching the arcs at the two vertical tangents uses one relative constant and leaves a genuine condition on f. The overall constants are only translations.

(2) 'Polyeder kann nie verbogen werden ?!' (a polyhedron can never be bent). This is the rigidity of polyhedra. The '?!' records a doubt.

(3) HURWITZ'S PROBLEM. Among n-gons with area J, minimise S_μ = Σ a_i^μ over the side lengths a_i. As transcribed, Hilbert claims:
- for μ ≤ 1 the minimiser is the regular n-gon;
- for μ > 1, from the pentagon on, the regular polygon stops being optimal once μ exceeds some bound;
- so n = 5 is the first interesting case.
Useful facts (mine):
- A regular n-gon with side s has area A = n s^2/(4 tan(π/n)).
- For μ ≥ 1, the power-mean inequality gives Σ a_i^μ ≥ n^{1-μ}(Σ a_i)^μ.
- The polygonal isoperimetric inequality (Zenodorus/Lhuilier) gives Σ a_i ≥ n s_reg.
- Hence S_μ ≥ n s_reg^μ, with equality for the regular polygon.

(4) A rigid body with liquid-filled tubular channels rotating about a fixed point. This is a gyrostat-type problem, after a Bonn dissertation of 1888–90 by 'Serf?'. Hilbert proposes treating it with Klein's α,β,γ,δ, i.e. the Cayley–Klein (SU(2)) parameters of the rotation.

(5) A BERTRAND–DARBOUX–HALPHEN QUESTION. Take a time-independent (autonomous) planar force field. Suppose every trajectory, for every initial point and every speed below some bound, is closed. Must the field then be one of the two laws of Darboux and Halphen (1877)? Those are the central forces for which every orbit is a conic. The reference is Appell, Mécanique rationnelle I, pp. 372–378, which treats Bertrand's problem.

(6) A COUNTABLE REPRESENTING SYSTEM OF POLYNOMIALS. The proof is finished on the next page.
Claim: there are polynomials φ_1, φ_2, … such that every continuous f on a (tacitly compact) interval can be written f = Σ c_k φ_k.
Construction:
- Enumerate the integer-coefficient polynomials as ψ_1, ψ_2, ….
- Set φ = ψ_1; ψ_1,ψ_2; ψ_1,ψ_2,ψ_3; … (each block repeats all previous ψ's).
- By Weierstrass, choose a polynomial χ_n with |f − χ_n| < 1/(2n).
- Choose a rational-coefficient polynomial σ_n with |χ_n − σ_n| < 1/(2n). Then |f − σ_n| < 1/n.
- Write f = σ_1 + Σ_n (σ_{n+1} − σ_n).
- Each difference is a rational polynomial, so it equals (1/N)·ψ_k for some k. That ψ_k reappears in every later block.
- So the m-th difference can be placed on a φ in the m-th or a later block, with all other coefficients zero.
The partial sums are σ_n with zeros inserted, so the series converges uniformly to f.
errors: Item 1: closure of the curve is not achieved by choosing integration constants; those constants are translations (and matching data between the upper and lower arcs). Closure is a condition on the data: ∫ρ(θ)e^{iθ}dθ = 0 with ρ = 1/f. The same reciprocal issue affects the previous page. Minkowski's necessary conditions are ∫ α/K dω = 0, i.e. with the reciprocal Gauss curvature (the surface element) as weight, not ∫ f α dω with f = K, unless f is read as 1/K.
Item 3, as transcribed, is mathematically wrong. For μ ≥ 1 the regular n-gon is always the minimiser (power mean plus the polygonal isoperimetric inequality), so it cannot fail for large μ > 1.

Item 3, continued: for small 0 < μ < 1 the regular n-gon (n ≥ 4) is not minimal. Degenerating to a regular (n−1)-gon or a triangle with tiny extra sides gives a smaller sum. For n = 4, the triangle limit 3·s_3^μ beats the square 4·s_4^μ when μ < 2 ln(4/3)/ln(4/√3) ≈ 0.687.

Item 3, continued: so either the inequalities are reversed in the manuscript or transcription (regular for μ ≥ 1, failure for μ below some bound), or something else is meant. Even with reversed inequalities, failure already occurs at n = 4, not first at n = 5. The case could be rescued only if degenerate polygons are excluded and 'interesting' means a non-degenerate non-regular minimiser.

Item 5, as a conjecture, is false. The anisotropic oscillator F = (−x, −4y) is time-independent and conservative, and all its bounded orbits are closed (Lissajous 1:2 curves). It is not central and its orbits are not conics, so it is not of Darboux–Halphen type. Closed orbits do not force conic orbits once the force is not assumed central.

Item 6 (next page): the inequality |χ_n − σ_n| < 1/(2n) is written without absolute value bars. The interval must be compact for Weierstrass to apply; this is tacit. The resulting system is a representing system, not a basis: coefficients are not unique.

results.what: Plane Minkowski problem: a convex closed curve with prescribed curvature as a function of normal direction, obtained by quadrature, plus a closure condition
results.modern_name: Minkowski problem in the plane (Fourier condition on the radius-of-curvature function)
results.usually_credited_to: Minkowski (1897/1903); the planar case is classical

results.what: Doubt whether every polyhedron is rigid ('?!')
results.modern_name: Cauchy rigidity theorem (convex polyhedra) vs flexible polyhedra
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy 1813 (convex); Bricard 1897 (flexible self-intersecting octahedra); Connelly 1977 (embedded flexible polyhedron)

results.what: Hurwitz's problem: minimise the sum of μ-th powers of the sides of n-gons of fixed area; claimed threshold behaviour, with the pentagon as first interesting case
results.modern_name: Discrete isoperimetric-type extremal problem for polygons (power-mean variant)
results.usually_credited_to: Hurwitz (as Hilbert attributes it); polygonal isoperimetry to Zenodorus/Lhuilier/Steiner

results.what: Rotation of a rigid body with fluid-filled channels about a fixed point, proposed to be treated with Cayley–Klein parameters
results.modern_name: Gyrostat / rigid body with fluid-filled cavities; Cayley–Klein parameters
results.usually_credited_to: Zhukovsky 1885; Volterra 1899 (gyrostats); Klein & Sommerfeld, Theorie des Kreisels (1897ff) for the α,β,γ,δ

results.what: Question: do closed orbits for all initial data in an arbitrary autonomous force field force a Darboux–Halphen law?
results.modern_name: Generalised Bertrand problem / classification of systems with all orbits closed (superintegrability)
results.usually_credited_to: Bertrand 1873; Darboux and Halphen 1877; later superintegrability literature

results.what: A countable sequence of polynomials such that every continuous function is a series Σ c_k φ_k, via Weierstrass approximation and rational/integer-coefficient enumeration
results.modern_name: Representing (Darstellungs-) system in C[a,b]; consequence of Weierstrass approximation and separability

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a list of problems and remarks of the 1890s. Hilbert's doubt about polyhedral rigidity is mildly interesting given Bricard (1897) and Connelly (1977). The generalised Bertrand question is a reasonable but naive conjecture, refuted by the 1:2 anisotropic oscillator. The Hurwitz polygon claim appears garbled or incorrect as written. The polynomial-series construction is a routine corollary of Weierstrass. Nothing here anticipates a major later result.

checkable.asserts: With y'=p and curvature f(p): dp/dx = f(p)(1+p^2)^(3/2), so x = ∫dp/g(p) + const (y = ∫p dp/g + const).
Closure test ∫ρ cosθ = ∫ρ sinθ = 0 holds for ρ = 1 + a cos 2θ, so such data give a closed curve; ρ = 1 + a cos θ would fail.
Area formula for the regular n-gon; for n = 4 it gives s^2.
Threshold ≈ 0.687 below which a degenerate quadrilateral (equilateral triangle plus a vanishing side) beats the square for Σ a_i^μ at fixed area. This contradicts 'regular for μ ≤ 1'.
Negative value: for μ = 1/2 and area 1, the triangle limit beats the square.

checkable.asserts: The non-central field (-x,-4y) has all orbits closed (period 2π) but they are Lissajous curves, not conics. This is a counterexample to the conjecture in item 5.
A difference of rational polynomials is (1/N) times an integer-coefficient polynomial, so each telescoping term is c·ψ_k as in the next-page construction.
